title: The man who stretched out his staff over the Red Sea.
paragraphs: The man who stretched out his staff over the Red Sea.
The man through whom God had announced freedom to a nation of slaves.
But none of those memories can quench a child's thirst.
And that is where Exodus 17 takes us.
Not into a peaceful worship service.
Not into a comfortable gathering of people celebrating answered prayers.
But into a wilderness where fear is becoming anger, anger is becoming accusation, and accusation is becoming rebellion.
The people have already witnessed extraordinary miracles.
They saw God strike Egypt with judgment.
They saw Him deliver them from slavery.
They walked through the sea on dry ground.
They watched their enemies disappear beneath the waters.
They tasted bitter water made drinkable at Marah.
They received manna from heaven.
Yet now, standing at Rephidim without water, they begin to wonder whether the God who delivered them has brought them into the wilderness to die.
And before we condemn them too quickly, perhaps we should ask ourselves a painful question.
How many times have we remembered God's faithfulness yesterday, yet struggled to trust Him with today's unanswered need?
We remember how He carried us through the last crisis.
But when another one comes, fear begins speaking louder than memory.
We remember the prayer He answered.
But the prayer still unanswered keeps us awake at night.
We remember the door He opened.
But the door now closed makes us wonder whether He has forgotten our address.
And sometimes the question we are afraid to say aloud begins forming in the deepest part of our hearts.
"Lord, are You still here?"
That question is not foreign to Exodus 17.
In fact, it stands at the very center of the story.
Scripture tells us that the Israelites journeyed according to the commandment of the LORD and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink.
Do not overlook those words.
They were following God's command, and they still arrived at a place without water.
That single detail confronts a dangerous misunderstanding about faith.
We sometimes assume that if God is leading us, the journey should become easier.
If we are obedient, provision should arrive before desperation.
If we are praying, suffering should disappear.
If we are walking with Christ, there should always be a visible explanation for what happens next.
But Israel did not arrive at Rephidim because they had wandered outside God's guidance.
Exodus 17:1 explicitly says they traveled according to His command.
The absence of water was real.
Their need was legitimate.
Their suffering was not imaginary.
Yet their circumstances were not evidence that God had lost control.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
You can be sincerely following Jesus and still face a season you do not understand.
You can be faithful in prayer and still receive a frightening medical report.
You can serve others and still experience financial hardship.
You can love your family and still watch relationships fracture.
You can be doing what is right and still find yourself asking why the road has become so difficult.
The wilderness does not automatically mean you have wandered away from God.
Sometimes it is the very place where your understanding of His faithfulness must grow beyond what you can see.
But there is another truth here, and it is not comfortable.
Having a legitimate need does not justify every response we make to that need.
Exodus 17:2 records the people's demand:
"Give us water that we may drink."
Moses responds by asking why they quarrel with him and why they test the LORD.
The Hebrew verb used for their quarreling is connected with רִיב (riv), a word associated with contention, dispute, and conflict.
This was not merely a quiet request for assistance.
The people were entering into a confrontation with Moses.
And behind their confrontation with Moses stood a far more serious question about God Himself.
By verse 3, their accusation becomes unmistakable.
They ask why Moses brought them out of Egypt to kill them, their children, and their livestock with thirst.
Think about the tragedy of that accusation.
The God who rescued them from death is now being accused of intending their death.
The deliverance they once celebrated is being reinterpreted as a betrayal.
Fear has begun rewriting their memory.
And that is one of the most dangerous things fear can do to a human heart.
It can make yesterday's mercy look meaningless because today's need remains unmet.
It can make us interpret God's silence as hostility.
It can turn a difficult season into a verdict against His character.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You once prayed with confidence.
Now you struggle to find words.
You once worshiped with joy.
Now you sit through a song while quietly fighting tears.
You once told people that God would make a way.
Now you are wondering why the way has not appeared for you.
And perhaps you feel ashamed because you have questions you think a mature Christian should never ask.
But listen carefully.
Scripture does not require you to pretend that thirst is not real.
It does not command you to deny grief, exhaustion, uncertainty, or pain.
The Psalms are filled with honest cries to God.
Jesus Himself prayed in deep anguish in Gethsemane.
The problem at Rephidim was not that the Israelites needed water or that they were distressed.
The problem was that their distress had become an accusation against the faithfulness of the God who had already shown them His saving power.
There is a difference between bringing your pain to God and putting God on trial as though He must prove Himself worthy of trust.
One is the cry of dependence.
The other demands that God submit to our judgment.
And the Israelites were crossing that line.
The crisis becomes so severe that Moses cries out to the LORD, asking what he should do with the people because they are nearly ready to stone him.
Imagine the loneliness of that moment.
Moses is standing between a desperate people and the God they are accusing.
He cannot manufacture water.
He cannot calm every frightened heart.
He cannot solve the crisis through charisma, leadership experience, or human strength.
He has reached the end of what he can do.
So he cries to God.
And what happens next is astonishing.
God does not tell Moses to abandon the people.
He does not instruct him to lead only the grateful Israelites into safety.
He does not announce that their failure has exhausted His mercy.
Instead, He gives Moses instructions.
Take the staff.
Gather some of the elders.
Go to the rock at Horeb.
And strike it.
But before the staff ever touches the stone, God says something extraordinary.
In Exodus 17:6, the LORD declares:
הִנְנִי עֹמֵד לְפָנֶיךָ שָּׁם עַל־הַצּוּר בְּחֹרֵב
Hineni omed lefanekha sham al-hatsur be-Chorev.
A close English rendering is:
"Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb."
Read that again.
God does not merely say, "I will send water."
He says He will stand there.
Before Moses.
On the rock.
At Horeb.
The Hebrew word הִנְנִי (hineni) carries the sense of "Behold, I am here" or "Here I am," calling attention to the speaker's presence and what He is about to do.
And the phrase עֹמֵד לְפָנֶיךָ (omed lefanekha) means "standing before you."
This is not a minor detail.
The people have been questioning whether God is among them.
And God announces His presence at the very place where He is about to provide for them.
The One they have accused has not disappeared.
The One whose faithfulness they have questioned is still acting for their good.
The One who delivered them from Egypt is not finished caring for them in the wilderness.
Then Moses strikes the rock as God commanded.
And water comes out.
Not from a spring the people had discovered.
Not from a well they had dug.
Not from a river flowing nearby.
From a rock.
In the wilderness.
At the command of the living God.
Imagine the first person who sees it.
Perhaps there is disbelief.
Then shouting.
Then people rushing forward with their containers.
Perhaps a father kneels to collect water for his child.
Perhaps a mother brings a drink to someone too weak to walk.
Perhaps the sound of flowing water begins to drown out the accusations that had filled the camp.
The text does not describe these individual reactions, and we should not pretend it does.
But the miracle itself is clear.
God provided water where His people had no visible means of obtaining it.
And He did so for a people who had just challenged His faithfulness.
That is what makes the miracle so powerful.
It is not simply a story about God's ability to provide.
It is also a revelation of His mercy toward undeserving people.
They were quarreling, and God gave them water.
They were testing Him, and God sustained their lives.
They were questioning His presence, and He revealed that He had not abandoned them.
Does that sound familiar?
It should.
Because the Bible is telling a much larger story.
A story that does not end at Horeb.
A story that leads us to Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Moses struck the rock, the apostle Paul wrote to the church in Corinth about Israel's wilderness experience.
In 1 Corinthians 10:4, he says:
ἡ δὲ πέτρα ἦν ὁ Χριστός
Hē de petra ēn ho Christos.
"And the Rock was Christ."
Those words should stop us.
Paul is not saying that Jesus was merely an ordinary geological rock.
Nor is he teaching that the physical stone was literally transformed into the incarnate Jesus.
He is interpreting Israel's wilderness provision in light of Christ, identifying Him as the ultimate spiritual source of the life-giving provision represented in the wilderness story.
Paul writes that the Israelites drank from the spiritual Rock that accompanied them, and that Rock was Christ.
The Greek word πέτρα (petra) means "rock."
And Paul deliberately connects that rock imagery to Christ.
What happened at Horeb was not an isolated miracle with no relationship to the rest of Scripture.
It belonged to the unfolding history of God's redemption.
The God who sustained Israel in the wilderness would reveal the fullness of His saving purpose through His Son.
But there is an important distinction we must preserve.
Exodus 17 does not explicitly state that the striking of the rock was a direct prediction of Jesus being struck at Calvary.
That connection is a theological reading Christians may draw from the wider biblical story, especially Paul's identification of Christ with the spiritual Rock.
We should not claim more than Scripture says.
Yet the parallel is profound.
At Horeb, God provided life-giving water for people who had rebelled against Him.
At Calvary, God provided salvation through Jesus Christ for sinners who could never save themselves.
At Horeb, thirsty people received what they could not produce.
At the cross, guilty people are offered forgiveness they could never earn.
At Horeb, the provision came from God's initiative.
At Calvary, redemption came through God's grace.
And there is something even more extraordinary.
The same Jesus whom Paul identifies with the spiritual Rock would one day stand before another thirsty human being.
Not in the wilderness of Sinai.
But beside a well in Samaria.
In John 4, Jesus meets a woman whose life is marked by complicated relationships and deep spiritual need.
He asks her for a drink.
Then He begins speaking about a kind of water no ordinary well can supply.
In John 4:14, Jesus teaches that whoever drinks the water He gives will never thirst in the same ultimate sense, because His gift becomes a spring welling up to eternal life.
The woman came looking for ordinary water.
Jesus offered her living water.
She came carrying the realities of her past.
Jesus spoke to her with truth and offered her something greater than the life she had known.
He did not pretend that her history did not exist.
He knew it.
Yet He continued speaking with her.
And through that encounter, many in her town eventually came to believe in Him.
Do you see the beauty?
At Horeb, God provided water for thirsty Israelites.
At the well, Jesus offered living water to a spiritually thirsty Samaritan woman.
And in John 7:37–39, Jesus openly invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, connecting that promise with the Holy Spirit whom believers would receive.
The physical miracle at Horeb sustained earthly life.
The living water Jesus gives speaks of something infinitely greater: the eternal life and spiritual renewal that come through Him.
One does not erase the other.
The first reveals God's care for real human need.
The second reveals the fullness of His saving grace.
And now the question becomes personal.
What kind of thirst have you been trying to satisfy without Jesus?
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you are worthy of love.
You keep achieving.
Keep working.
Keep smiling.
Keep making sure nobody sees how tired you really are.
But when the room becomes quiet, you still feel empty.
Perhaps you have been chasing approval.
Every compliment gives you relief for a moment.
Every rejection wounds you more deeply than you want to admit.
And no matter how much attention you receive, it never seems to be enough.
Perhaps you have been trying to bury guilt beneath distractions.
You tell yourself that what happened was years ago.
That you have changed.
That you should stop thinking about it.
Yet something inside you still longs to know whether forgiveness is truly possible.
Or perhaps your thirst is not connected to a scandalous past at all.
Perhaps you are simply exhausted.
Exhausted from being the strong one.
Exhausted from carrying responsibilities.
Exhausted from praying for someone who seems determined to walk away from God.
Exhausted from trying to remain faithful while your circumstances keep getting worse.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
And somewhere deep inside, you are asking the same question Israel asked at Rephidim.
"Is the LORD among us, or not?"
Those are the words of Exodus 17:7.
And they reveal why Moses gave the place two significant names.
מַסָּה (Massah) — "testing."
מְרִיבָה (Meribah) — "quarreling" or "contention."
These names memorialized the people's testing of God and their dispute with Moses.
The place was not named simply to celebrate the water.
It also preserved the memory of Israel's failure.
That matters.
Because the Bible refuses to turn the people of God into flawless heroes.
It tells the truth about them.
Their fear.
Their unbelief.
Their rebellion.
Their need.
And God's mercy.
This is why the Gospel is so different from the message that says, "Become good enough, and then God will accept you."
The Gospel announces that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ, not through their own moral achievements.
Romans 5:8 says that God demonstrates His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we repaired every broken part of our lives.
Not after we learned to hide our failures more convincingly.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve heaven.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not mean sin is harmless.
It does not mean repentance is optional.
It does not mean grace gives us permission to continue rebelling against God.
True grace does not merely comfort us while leaving us unchanged.
It calls us to turn from sin and trust the Savior.
It forgives.
It restores.
It transforms.
It teaches us to say no to ungodliness and to live in the light of Christ.
And this is where the story at Horeb becomes both comforting and confronting.
God's provision did not make Israel's unbelief acceptable.
His mercy did not mean their accusations were justified.
Later, Psalm 95 would warn God's people not to harden their hearts as Israel did at Meribah and Massah.
Hebrews 3 takes that warning seriously and urges believers not to develop an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
The water was a gift.
But the hardened heart remained a danger.
And perhaps that is the warning some of us need today.
You can receive blessings from God while resisting the very transformation He is calling you to embrace.
You can enjoy His provision while refusing His correction.
You can speak about His goodness publicly while quietly defending sin privately.
You can know the language of Christianity without surrendering the deepest parts of your life to Christ.
And no amount of religious activity can substitute for genuine repentance and faith.
That is why the question is not simply whether God can bring water from your rock.
The deeper question is whether you will trust Him, listen to His Word, and allow His grace to change you.
Because not every difficult circumstance disappears immediately when we pray.
Not every illness is healed in this life.
Not every financial problem ends with an unexpected provision.
Not every broken relationship is restored on the timeline we desire.
Exodus 17 is a historical account of a specific miracle, not a guarantee that God will resolve every modern crisis in the same miraculous way.
But the Gospel gives believers a greater assurance.
Through Jesus Christ, God has acted decisively for our salvation.
And those who belong to Christ are not abandoned, even when their circumstances remain painful.
That is why faith must be anchored in God's character, not merely in the speed of His answers.
Consider Moses again.
When the people threatened him, he cried to God.
He did not pretend to possess the answer.
He did not manufacture a miracle.
He turned toward the only One who could provide what the people needed.
There is a lesson in that for every exhausted parent, struggling believer, overwhelmed leader, and wounded soul reading these words.
You do not have to pretend you are the source.
You are not the Savior.
You are not the one who can repair every heart, solve every crisis, or carry every burden without help.
There is only one Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And the Christian life was never meant to be sustained by self-sufficiency.
It is sustained by grace.
Perhaps the most important thing you can do today is stop pretending you have enough strength for everything.
Bring your need honestly before God.
Confess where fear has become unbelief.
Repent where pain has become bitterness.
Ask forgiveness where disappointment has led you into sin.
And trust the Lord who has already revealed His love through the cross and resurrection of His Son.
There is another detail we should not miss.
The staff Moses carried to Horeb was the same staff associated with God's mighty acts in Egypt.
Exodus 17:5 specifically identifies it as the staff with which Moses struck the Nile.
Think about that contrast.
In Egypt, the striking of the Nile was associated with judgment, as the river's water turned to blood.
At Horeb, the striking of the rock was followed by water that sustained the people.
The same God who judges evil is also the God who mercifully provides.
His holiness and His compassion are not enemies.
And at the cross of Jesus Christ, we see the deepest revelation of God's righteousness and saving love.
Sin is not dismissed as insignificant.
It is dealt with through the sacrifice of Christ.
Grace is not God pretending evil does not matter.
Grace is God providing salvation at a cost we could never pay.
This is why we must never reduce the Gospel to a motivational message about getting through hard times.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult lives more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
That is the heart of everything.
Not a rock.
Not a wilderness.
Not even a miracle.
Jesus Christ.
The miracle points beyond itself to the God whose redemptive purposes culminate in Him.
And if you are reading this while carrying a hidden burden, I want you to hear something.
Your past does not have to be the final word over your life.
Your worst failure does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your deepest shame does not have to remain your lifelong prison.
There is forgiveness in Christ for those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
There is mercy for the guilty.
There is restoration for the repentant.
There is hope for the weary.
There is new life through the risen Savior.
That does not mean every consequence of the past disappears.
It means the past no longer has authority to declare that redemption is impossible.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by denying what happened.
Not by calling evil good.
But by forgiving sinners, transforming hearts, and making new creations out of people who could never rescue themselves.
And perhaps you have spent too long believing that your story is already ruined.
Perhaps you think your marriage has suffered too much.
Your family has seen too much.
Your reputation has fallen too far.
Your faith has grown too weak.
Your prayers have been too inconsistent.
Your sins have been too many.
But if you are still breathing, the invitation to turn to Christ remains before you.
Do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
Conviction calls you toward repentance.
Hopelessness tells you not to bother.
The Gospel calls you to come to Jesus.
And He is not a Savior who requires you to clean yourself up before you are allowed to ask for mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting in His finished work.
Come because He alone can give the life you cannot produce for yourself.
And if you have already trusted Him, return to the truth you may have forgotten in the middle of your wilderness.
The Lord who saved you has not ceased to be faithful.
Even when you cannot understand the road.
Even when the next step frightens you.
Even when your prayers are mixed with tears.
Even when you must wait longer than you expected.
The presence of difficulty is not proof of the absence of God.
And His grace is not measured by how comfortable your circumstances become.
One day, the temporary thirsts and sufferings of this present world will give way to something glorious for all who belong to Christ.
Revelation 7:17 declares that the Lamb will shepherd His people and guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
Notice who stands at the center of that promise.
The Lamb.
Jesus.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One who conquered death.
The One who will bring His redeemed people into the fullness of God's presence.
At Horeb, water flowed to sustain people in the wilderness.
In Revelation, the Lamb leads His people to the springs of living water.
And between those two scenes stands the cross and the empty tomb.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected inspirational moments.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's saving purpose, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
That is why this story matters.
It is not simply asking whether God can provide water from a rock.
It is inviting us to recognize the God who is faithful, holy, merciful, and worthy of our trust.
It is warning us against hardening our hearts.
It is exposing the danger of allowing fear to rewrite what we know about God's character.
And through the New Testament's witness, it directs our attention to Christ, the true source of spiritual life.
Maybe you began reading this because you were curious about an ancient miracle.
But perhaps somewhere along the way, the story began reading you.
Perhaps you recognized your own fear in Israel's accusations.
Your exhaustion in Moses' desperate prayer.
Your spiritual thirst in the empty containers of the wilderness.
Your need for grace in the mercy God extended to an undeserving people.
And perhaps you now realize that the most important question is not, "Why did God make water flow from a rock?"
The most important question is, "What will I do with the Christ to whom Scripture points?"
Will you continue running from Him?
Will you continue hiding behind religious appearances?
Will you continue postponing repentance?
Or will you surrender?
Not because you have everything figured out.
Not because you are finally strong enough.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
If this message has exposed something you have been carrying in silence, you do not have to pretend.
You can pray right where you are.

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I have allowed fear, disappointment, and sin to shape the way I see You. Forgive me for the times I have doubted Your goodness and hardened my heart against Your Word. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, turn away from sin, and follow You faithfully. When I cannot see the way forward, help me remember who You are. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen."
And if those words express the surrender your heart is longing for, do not let this moment pass without responding.
You do not have to share the details of your struggle publicly. But sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of encouragement, prayer, and genuine fellowship.
Someone reading may be standing where you once stood.
They may need to hear that faithfulness is possible even when the road is painful.
They may need to know that repentance is not the end of hope.
They may need to be reminded that Christ still saves, restores, and transforms lives.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious language.
Not to turn the Gospel into a product.
Not to replace the local church, pastoral care, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep placing Scripture-centered messages before people who need to hear the truth about Jesus Christ.
People who are hurting.
People who are searching.
People who have drifted from faith.
People who are ashamed of their past.
People who are curious about Christianity but do not know where to begin.
And people who have followed Christ for years yet still need daily encouragement, correction, and spiritual nourishment.
The mission is to point hearts back to Jesus.
Again and again.
Because a world filled with noise desperately needs the truth of God's Word.
And this is where you can become part of that mission.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
Not because your salvation, blessings, or spiritual standing depend on financial support.
They do not.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not through payments, donations, or religious transactions.
But voluntary, cheerful financial support for Gospel ministry is a meaningful way believers may participate in the work of spreading God's Word.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

Philippians 4:15–17 also shows how believers participated in supporting the apostle Paul's ministry, while Paul emphasized the spiritual fruit of their generosity rather than treating their gifts as a purchase of God's favor.
If you choose to include that support within your personal giving budget, do so prayerfully and responsibly, without neglecting your family, your local church, or other important obligations.
The greatest reason to partner is the opportunity to help more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Because the Word of God should never be reduced to something only paying supporters are allowed to receive.
And there is room for the believer who cannot.
There is room for the person whose faith is strong today.
And there is room for the person who is barely holding on.
What matters most is that we keep pointing one another to Jesus.
And you can help even without spending anything.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen, but because someone among your friends or family may be struggling with the very questions raised in Exodus 17.
Someone may be silently wondering whether God has abandoned them.
Someone may be living with guilt and needs to hear the Gospel of grace.
Someone may have stopped praying because they no longer believe God is listening.
You do not know who may read it.
But you can make the message available.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, spiritual seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along and explore the message of Jesus Christ.
Not everyone who reads will immediately believe.
Not everyone will respond.
But every person deserves to hear the Gospel presented with truth, compassion, and faithfulness to Scripture.
And before you leave, remember the people standing at Horeb.
They had no water.
They had no visible solution.
They had reached a place where human resources were insufficient.
But the story did not end with empty containers.
God was present.
God spoke.
God provided.
And generations later, the apostle Paul would direct believers to Christ through the imagery of that wilderness Rock.
So when you return to your own difficult circumstances, do not carry away only the thought that God once performed an extraordinary miracle.
Carry away the greater truth.
The God who provided for Israel has revealed His saving grace in Jesus Christ.
And the Savior who died and rose again is worthy of your faith, your repentance, your worship, and your life.
You may not know how tomorrow will unfold.
You may not know when the burden will become lighter.
You may not know why this particular road has been so painful.
But you can know the One who has conquered sin and death.
And in Him, your story is not defined by the worst thing you have done, the hardest thing you have suffered, or the darkest place you have walked through.
Your hope is anchored in what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
The wilderness may expose how empty your hands are, but the cross reveals how full God's mercy is.
